title: Boreas. Zetes et Calais
titleEn: Boreas and Orithyia; Zetes and Calais — Metamorphoses VI.675–721
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 fb3fdb1d8a4a3b82. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Grief kills Pandion, and Erechtheus takes the sceptre after him, with four sons and four daughters, two of them matched in beauty. One is Procris, happily married to Cephalus; the other is Orithyia, whom Boreas the north wind wants — and Tereus and the Thracians tell against him, so his asking gets nothing. Then he stops asking: a speech arguing that force is what he is made for, and he shakes out his wings, sweeps the ground with a cloak of dust and carries Orithyia off to the country of the Cicones. There she becomes the wife of the freezing tyrant and the mother of Calais and Zetes, who come to their wings late and then sail with the Minyae after the golden fleece, over an unknown sea, in the first ship ever built.

advisory.lede: Boreas is refused Orithyia, argues that force is what he is made for, and carries her off terrified — an abduction whose end is rape, which the poem then records as a marriage.
advisory.more: The poem gives Boreas a speech of fifteen lines in which he says plainly that asking was the mistake and that violence is his proper nature, and no one in the poem rebuts it: he acts on it in the very next sentence, and the narrator's only remark is that whatever Boreas said was no lower in pitch than this. Ovid's own nouns track what happens closely. At the moment of the seizure he is 'amans', the lover; three lines later he is 'raptor', the word Latin uses of a man who carries a woman off and of a rapist. What is done to Orithyia is never narrated. What follows is: she is called the wife of the freezing tyrant and the mother of his twin sons, and the poem moves on to the sons. Lectorium presents the text unaltered.

sentences.t:
Hic dolor ante diem longaeque extrema senectae
tempora Tartareas Pandiona misit ad umbras.
sentences.l: This grief sent Pandion to the Tartarean shades before his day and before the last season of a long old age.
sentences.i: Grief sent Pandion down among the shades of Tartarus before his time, before ever he reached the last season of a long old age.
sentences.n: 'Hic dolor' — 'this grief' — points back at what the previous lines have just told, and the part opens on its aftermath: a king is buried in two lines, with no scene. Pandion is the king whose place Erechtheus takes in the next line. 'ante diem' is the standing Latin phrase for dying before one's appointed day, and 'ante' governs 'tempora' as well as 'diem', so the one idea is said twice over. In 676 'Tartareas ... ad umbras' is split around 'Pandiona misit', so the adjective arrives long before the noun it belongs to and the shades close the line. 'Pandiona' is a Greek accusative; Greek names keep their Greek endings in Latin verse.

sentences.t:
Sceptra loci rerumque capit moderamen Erechtheus,
iustitia dubium validisne potentior armis.
sentences.l: Erechtheus takes up the sceptres of the place and the steering of affairs — a doubtful thing, whether he was the more powerful in justice or in strong arms.
sentences.i: Erechtheus takes the sceptre of the country and the running of the state, and it is hard to say whether he was the stronger in justice or in force of arms.
sentences.n: 'Sceptra' is plural for singular, as Latin regularly is with the insignia of office. 'rerum moderamen' is 'the steering of affairs': 'res' in the plural is the ordinary word for public business, and 'moderamen' is properly the tiller of a ship. 'dubium' is a bare neuter adjective dropped in with no verb — 'a doubtful thing' — and English has to supply 'it is uncertain'. What follows is a double question with the first limb unmarked and '-ne' hung on the second: 'iustitia ... validisne ... armis' is 'whether by justice or by strong arms'. The compliment cuts both ways, and it is placed here on purpose: the man credited with justice and with arms in the same breath is the one Boreas will say at 701 should have been forced rather than asked.

sentences.t:
Quattuor ille quidem iuvenes totidemque crearat
femineae sortis: sed erat par forma duarum.
sentences.l: He had indeed fathered four young men and just as many of the female lot: but the beauty of two was equal.
sentences.i: He had fathered four sons, true enough, and as many daughters — but two of them were matched in beauty.
sentences.n: 'crearat' is syncopated 'creaverat', a pluperfect: the children were there before the reign just described. 'quidem' concedes the whole eight before 'sed' narrows the sentence to the two that matter. 'femineae sortis' is a genitive of description, 'of the female lot' — the daughters get no noun of their own but are counted by 'totidem', 'just as many', and named by their sex. 'par forma duarum' is the hinge: 'par' does not say that the two were beautiful but that they were equally so, which is what lets the poem set them side by side in the lines that follow.

sentences.t:
E quibus Aeolides Cephalus te coniuge felix,
Procri, fuit;
sentences.l: Of these, Cephalus of Aeolus' line was happy with you as his wife, Procris;
sentences.n: 'E quibus' is a connecting relative opening the sentence — 'and of these', the two matched sisters — which English turns into an ordinary phrase. 'te coniuge' is a bare two-word ablative, noun and predicate noun with no verb: 'with you as wife'. It can be taken as an ablative absolute of the barest kind, but it more probably hangs on 'felix', which regularly governs an ablative of the thing one is fortunate in — happy in her. And 'Procri' is a vocative, a Greek one: the poem stops narrating and speaks to her. This turning aside to address a character is called apostrophe, and it is the reader's signal that the poem is not neutral about the person addressed. 'Aeolides' is a Greek patronymic, 'of the line of Aeolus'.

sentences.t:
Boreae Tereus Thracesque nocebant,
dilectaque diu caruit deus Orithyia,
dum rogat et precibus mavult quam viribus uti.
sentences.l: Tereus and the Thracians were doing Boreas harm, and the god went long without his beloved Orithyia, while he asks and prefers to use entreaties rather than force.
sentences.i: Tereus and the Thracians were what told against Boreas, and the god went a long time without the Orithyia he loved — for as long as he was asking, and preferred prayers to force.
sentences.n: 'Boreae' is a dative with 'nocebant': they were doing harm to Boreas. The harm is by association — Boreas is the north wind and his country is Thrace, so a Thracian and his people had made a Thracian suitor hateful where Orithyia lived. 'caruit' takes an ablative of the thing gone without, 'dilecta ... Orithyia', with the two words pushed to the ends of the phrase and 'diu' and the verb shut between them: the length of the wait is written into the word order. 'dum' with the present indicative 'rogat' inside a perfect narrative is the ordinary 'so long as', and it carries the whole point — the asking is what cost him the time. 'uti' takes an ablative, and the pair it governs, 'precibus' against 'viribus', is the argument of the speech that follows, set out before he opens his mouth.

sentences.t:
Ast ubi blanditiis agitur nihil, horridus ira,
quae solita est illi nimiumque domestica vento,
“et merito!” dixit:
sentences.l: But when nothing is got done by coaxing, bristling with anger — which is habitual to him and all too much at home in that wind — 'and deservedly!' he said.
sentences.i: But when soft words got him nowhere, bristling with the rage that is his habit and all too much at home in that wind, 'and serve me right!' he said.
sentences.n: 'Ast' is an old, high-style form of 'at', 'but'. 'agitur' is passive with 'nihil' as its subject — 'nothing is being got done' — and 'blanditiis' is the ablative of means: 'blanditiae' are coaxing, wheedling words, the language of a lover, which is exactly the register he is about to renounce. 'horridus' is the physical word for bristling, hair or water standing up, and given to a wind it is his temper and his weather in one adjective. The relative 'quae' picks up 'ira', and 'illi ... vento' is one dative phrase serving both adjectives, 'to that wind of his', which English has to spread across two complements — so the anger belongs to him because of what he is, with 'nimium', 'too much', doing the judging. 'et merito' is elliptical, 'and deservedly [it happened]': the first thing he says is that his failure was his own fault, and the rest of the speech explains why.

sentences.t:
“quid enim mea tela reliqui,
saevitiam et vires iramque animosque minaces,
admovique preces, quarum me dedecet usus?
sentences.l: 'For why did I abandon my weapons — savagery and strength and anger and threatening spirits — and bring up entreaties, the use of which disgraces me?'
sentences.i: 'Why did I ever put my own weapons down — savagery, strength, rage, a threatening temper — and bring prayers up in their place, when the use of them is beneath me?'
sentences.n: 'quid' here is 'why', an accusative doing adverbial work, and 'enim' explains the 'merito' just before: this is the reason he says he deserved it. The four accusatives of 688 stand in apposition to 'mea tela' — his armoury is a list of temperaments, not of objects, which is the claim the whole speech rests on. 'admovi' is a siege word: you 'bring up' engines against a wall, so even his begging is put in the vocabulary of assault. 'dedecet' is usually met impersonally, 'it is unbecoming', but here it has an expressed subject: the person disgraced stands in the accusative ('me') and the thing that disgraces is the nominative subject ('usus'). The shame he names is in the using of prayers, not in what he was asking for. 'quarum' is an ordinary relative, a genitive with 'usus' and 'preces' as its antecedent — not the connecting relative that opens a sentence, which is what 'quarum' does at 703.

sentences.t: Apta mihi vis est:
sentences.l: 'Fitting for me is force:'
sentences.i: 'Force is what suits me:'
sentences.n: The thesis of the speech, four words. The predicate adjective 'apta' comes first, before its subject, so the sentence lands on 'fitting'; the literal keeps that order to show where the weight falls, and the idiomatic puts it back the English way. 'vis' is force in the widest sense — the strength of a wind and the violence done to a person — and the one word covers both here, at the two 'vi' ablatives that open the next clauses, and again at 701, where it is the means he says should have got him the marriage.

sentences.t:
vi tristia nubila pello,
vi freta concutio nodosaque robora verto
induroque nives et terras grandine pulso.
sentences.l: 'by force I drive off the grim clouds, by force I shake the straits and overturn the knotted oaks, and I harden the snows and beat the lands with hail.'
sentences.i: 'By force I drive the sullen clouds away; by force I shake the seas and throw down knotted oaks; I pack the snow hard and hammer the earth with hail.'
sentences.n: The repeated 'vi ... vi' at the head of two clauses is the engine of the speech: the same ablative of means, struck twice, so that the instrument and the nature are one thing. 'tristia' of clouds is 'grim, sullen', a word for a person's mood handed to the weather. 'robora' is properly hard oak-wood, so 'nodosa robora' names the trees by their timber. 'induro' is 'I make hard', snow set into ice. 'pulso' is the frequentative of the 'pello' that opened the run: he drives the clouds off once and then keeps on striking the ground, and the two verbs are the same root at two intensities.

sentences.t:
Idem ego cum fratres caelo sum nactus aperto
(nam mihi campus is est), tanto molimine luctor,
ut medius nostris concursibus insonet aether
exsiliantque cavis elisi nubibus ignes.
sentences.l: 'I, the same one, when I have come upon my brothers in the open sky (for that is my field), wrestle with such heaving that the middle air rings with our runnings-together and fires leap out, struck from the hollow clouds.'
sentences.i: 'And when I meet my brothers out in the open sky — that is my wrestling-ground — I wrestle so hugely that the air between rings with the clash of us, and fire leaps out, struck from the hollow clouds.'
sentences.n: 'Idem ego' is 'I, the same one': he is showing that a single nature does all of this, and the phrase comes back at 697 to open the next item. 'sum nactus' is 'nanciscor', a deponent — passive in form, active in meaning — 'I have come upon, got hold of', with 'fratres' as its object; the brothers are the other winds. 'caelo ... aperto' is an ablative of place split around the verb. 'campus' is the open ground where Romans exercised and wrestled, which is why 'luctor', 'I wrestle', follows: a storm is put as a match on a field. 'tanto molimine' is an ablative of manner, 'molimen' being heaving effort, the strain of shifting something enormous, and it sets up a result clause with two subjunctives sharing one 'ut', 'insonet' and 'exsiliant'. 'elisi' is 'squeezed out, struck out': lightning here is fire crushed out of a cloud by the collision.

sentences.t:
Idem ego cum subii convexa foramina terrae
supposuique ferox imis mea terga cavernis,
sollicito manes totumque tremoribus orbem.
sentences.l: 'I, the same one, when I have gone in under the arched hollows of the earth and, fierce, set my back beneath the lowest caverns, trouble the dead and the whole globe with tremblings.'
sentences.i: 'And when I have gone in under the vaulted hollows of the earth and put my back, fierce as I am, under the lowest caves, I shake the dead and the whole world with earthquakes.'
sentences.n: The second 'Idem ego', built on the same frame as 693 — one 'cum' clause, one main verb — so that sky and underworld answer each other. 'subii' is 'sub-eo', 'I go in under', taking 'foramina' as its goal in the accusative; 'convexa' is 'arched, vaulted', the underground read as a roof he can get a shoulder to. 'ferox' is a nominative adjective doing the work of an English adverb: Latin prefers to say what a man is rather than how he acts, and both layers keep him fierce rather than merely acting fiercely. 'imis ... cavernis' is a dative with 'supposui' naming what he heaves his back up under; 'mea terga' is the accusative, the thing actually put beneath them. 'manes' are the shades of the dead — he is claiming that the shaking reaches even them. The earthquake here is wind shut in underground and heaving upward, which is how the poem accounts for it.

sentences.t:
Hac ope debueram thalamos petiisse, socerque
non orandus erat, vi sed faciendus Erechtheus.”
sentences.l: 'With this power I ought to have gone after the marriage-chamber, and Erechtheus was not to be begged as a father-in-law, but made one by force.'
sentences.i: 'That was the strength I should have gone to the marriage-bed with; Erechtheus was not to be begged into becoming my father-in-law — he was to be made one by force.'
sentences.n: 'debueram' is a pluperfect indicative where English needs 'I ought to have': Latin puts the obligation into the tense of the verb and leaves the infinitive to carry the deed, so 'debueram petiisse' is 'I ought to have sought'. 'petiisse' is syncopated 'petivisse'. 'thalamos' is the marriage-chamber, plural for singular, standing for the marriage itself. 'orandus' and 'faciendus' are gerundives of obligation with 'erat' — 'was to be begged', 'was to be made' — and the whole sentence turns on that pair: the same man is either asked or manufactured, and the second is what he now says he should have done. 'hac ope' is an ablative of means gathering the entire storm-and-earthquake catalogue into one instrument. Magnus prints 'vi', 'by force', which names the means and answers the 'precibus ... viribus' of 684; the second witness prints 'mihi', which stands in the second limb only and can be read either as a dative of agent with the gerundive ('made by me') or as the person for whom ('made my father-in-law'); on either reading the means goes unsaid. Magnus's reading is the one that closes the argument the speech has been making, and it is the reading translated here.

sentences.t:
Haec Boreas aut his non inferiora locutus
excussit pennas:
sentences.l: Boreas, having spoken these things or things not lower than these, shook out his wings:
sentences.i: Boreas said this, or something no less violent, and shook his wings out:
sentences.n: 'locutus' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'loquor' — passive in form, active in meaning, 'having spoken'. 'Haec ... aut his non inferiora' is the poet standing back from his own report: he will not swear these were the words, only that whatever was said was no lower in pitch. 'inferiora' is a comparative neuter plural with 'his' as its ablative of comparison, and the litotes — 'not lower' for 'quite as bad' — is the narrator's one dry verdict on the speech: it judges the pitch of what was said and answers none of its argument. 'excussit' is 'shook out, shook loose', and the wings are the weapon: he has spent the whole speech describing himself as weather, and this is the line where he stops describing and becomes it.

sentences.t:
quarum iactatibus omnis
adflata est tellus latumque perhorruit aequor.
sentences.l: at the tossings of these the whole earth was breathed upon and the broad sea shuddered all over.
sentences.i: Their beating blew across the whole earth, and the wide sea shivered from end to end.
sentences.n: 'quarum' is a connecting relative — 'and of these', the wings — where English uses a plain pronoun. 'iactatibus' is an ablative of means from an uncommon noun, 'tossings, brandishings'. 'adflata est' is the everyday verb for breathing on something, which is what a wind does; it stands passive here, with 'omnis ... tellus' as its subject, so the whole earth is the thing breathed on. 'perhorruit' carries the intensive 'per-': it is used of skin going up in gooseflesh and of water going rough under a wind, and both senses are live at once — the sea's surface is being treated as a skin.

sentences.t:
Pulvereamque trahens per summa cacumina pallam
verrit humum pavidamque metu caligine tectus
Orithyian amans fulvis amplectitur alis.
sentences.l: And dragging a cloak of dust over the highest treetops he sweeps the ground, and, wrapped in murk, the lover clasps Orithyia, frightened with fear, in his tawny wings.
sentences.i: Trailing a cloak of dust across the treetops he sweeps the ground, and, hidden in the murk, the lover folds Orithyia, shaking with terror, into his tawny wings.
sentences.n: 'palla' is a woman's long outer robe, and the dust the wind drags along the treetops is put on him as clothing; 'verrit humum', 'sweeps the ground', is what such a robe does when it trails, so the two lines are one image held steady. 'pavidam ... metu' is 'frightened with fear', an accusative agreeing with 'Orithyian' but cut off from it by 'caligine tectus' and the line-end, so that her terror is named before she is. 'Orithyian' is a Greek accusative. 'caligine tectus' is nominative and agrees with him: he covers himself in darkness first. 'amans', 'the lover', stands where a subject noun goes, and it is the poem's own word for him at this moment, not a character's — the act it introduces is an abduction. 'amplectitur' is a deponent, active in sense, and it is the verb both for an embrace and for a seizure; the difficulty of the passage is that Ovid will not choose between them. The tenses shift under the seizure: 'excussit' and 'adflata est' are perfect, then 'verrit' and 'amplectitur' go into the present and 'arserunt' and 'suppressit' fall back to the perfect — the historic present, putting the seizure in front of the reader as it happens.

sentences.t: Dum volat, arserunt agitati fortius ignes.
sentences.l: While he flies, his fires, stirred, burned the more strongly.
sentences.i: As he flew, the fire in him was fanned and burned harder.
sentences.n: 'ignes' in the plural is the standing metaphor for the fires of desire, and in this one line the metaphor turns literal: he is a wind, and 'agitati' — 'stirred, fanned' — is exactly what a wind does to a flame. Flight and appetite are made the same motion. 'Dum' with the present 'volat' inside a perfect narrative is the ordinary 'while'; the present tense holds because the flying is still going on around the burning.

sentences.t:
Nec prius aerii cursus suppressit habenas,
quam Ciconum tenuit populos et moenia raptor.
sentences.l: Nor did he check the reins of his airy course before the ravisher had reached the peoples and the walls of the Cicones.
sentences.i: The ravisher did not rein in his flight through the air until he had reached the Cicones, their people and their walls.
sentences.n: 'Nec prius ... quam' is one idiom split across the two lines, 'not before ... than': he never slowed until he arrived. 'aerii cursus ... habenas' makes the flight a chariot-team he is holding in, the reins belonging to the course itself. 'raptor' is the agent noun of 'rapio', the snatcher, the man who carries a woman off — the same word Latin uses of a rapist — and the poem holds it back to the end of the sentence and the end of the flight. Three lines earlier he was 'amans', the lover; this is the narrator's other word for the same man, and both layers keep it. 'Ciconum' is a genitive: the Cicones are a Thracian people, so the line names his own country before it names him — he has taken her home.

sentences.t:
Illic et gelidi coniunx Actaea tyranni
et genetrix facta est, partus enixa gemellos,
cetera qui matris, pennas genitoris haberent.
sentences.l: There the Attic woman was made both the wife of the freezing tyrant and a mother, having brought forth twin offspring, who had the mother's everything else, the father's wings.
sentences.i: There the woman of Attica became both wife of the freezing tyrant and mother, delivered of twin sons who had all the rest of themselves from her and their wings from him.
sentences.n: 'Actaea' is 'of Acte', the old name for Attica: she is named by her country rather than by her name, which these lines do not use again after the seizure at 707. 'coniunx ... et genetrix facta est' is the sentence that follows the abduction, and it calls the result a marriage without a word of comment; 'coniunx' covers wife and consort alike and passes no judgement. 'gelidi tyranni' is the poem's phrase for him — cold and absolute in two words; 'tyrannus' in verse is often no more than 'lord, monarch', and the harshness English hears in 'tyrant' is a choice made in the light of what has just happened rather than a fact carried by the noun. 'enixa' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'enitor', active in sense, 'having given birth'. 'haberent' is subjunctive in a relative clause of description — 'the sort who had' — defining what the twins were rather than reporting a fact about them. 'matris' and 'genitoris' are possessive genitives balanced against each other inside a single line, with 'cetera' and 'pennas' as the objects of 'haberent': everything else hers, the wings his.

sentences.t:
Non tamen has una memorant cum corpore natas,
barbaque dum rutilis aberat subnixa capillis,
implumes Calaisque puer Zetesque fuerunt.
sentences.l: Yet they do not recount that these were born together with the body; and while the beard, propped below their red hair, was still lacking, Calais the boy and Zetes were unfledged.
sentences.i: The wings, though, are not said to have been born with the body: while there was still no beard under their red hair, the boys Calais and Zetes went featherless.
sentences.n: 'memorant' is 'they tell, they recount', an indefinite third plural that puts the detail down to report rather than to the poem, and it takes an accusative and infinitive, 'has ... natas [esse]'. 'Non' stands first and negates 'memorant', not the infinitive: Latin denies the telling where English more naturally denies the thing told, which is what the idiomatic does. 'has' is the wings, carried over from the line before. 'una cum corpore' is 'at one and the same time as the body'. 'dum ... aberat' is 'while it was away', a 'dum' clause with the imperfect for a state that lasted a while. 'subnixa' is 'propped underneath': the beard sitting below the hair of the head, with 'rutilis', red-gold, the same colouring as the 'fulvis alis' of 707 — they take their father's colour before they take his wings. 'implumes' is 'unfledged', the word for a nestling still without feathers, and it is the predicate of both brothers; 'puer' is attached to Calais alone but covers the pair, which Latin verse does freely.

sentences.t:
Mox pariter pennae ritu coepere volucrum
cingere utrumque latus, pariter flavescere malae.
sentences.l: Soon, together, feathers began, after the manner of birds, to gird each side, and together the cheeks began to grow golden.
sentences.i: Soon, at one and the same time, feathers began to close round both their flanks the way a bird's do, and their cheeks began to turn gold.
sentences.n: 'coepere' is '-ēre' for '-ērunt', the poetic third-plural perfect; it comes again at 721 in 'petiere'. The one verb does duty for both halves of the sentence — 'pennae' is its subject in the first, 'malae' in the second, and the second 'began' has to be supplied in English. 'ritu' with a genitive is a fixed ablative, 'after the manner of', here 'as birds do'. 'utrumque latus' is 'each side' of each of them. 'flavescere' is an inchoative verb, the '-sc-' marking a process getting under way: not 'to be golden' but 'to start going gold', which is what a first beard does. 'pariter ... pariter' answers itself across the two halves — wings and beard arrive together, and the second is what tells you they are men now. Whether 'pariter' means the two brothers alike or the two changes at once is left open; both are true of the sentence.

sentences.t:
Ergo ubi concessit tempus puerile iuventae,
vellera cum Minyis nitido radiantia villo
per mare non notum prima petiere carina.
sentences.l: So when the boyish time had given way to young manhood, they made with the Minyae for the fleece radiant with gleaming wool, over a sea not known, in the first keel.
sentences.i: So when their boyhood had given way to young manhood, they sailed with the Minyae after the fleece that shines with gleaming wool, over a sea nobody knew, in the first ship there ever was.
sentences.n: 'concessit' with the dative 'iuventae' is 'gave place to': boyhood yields the ground to young manhood. 'petiere' is '-ēre' for '-ērunt' again, as 'coepere' was at 717. 'vellera' is plural for singular, the golden fleece, and 'radiantia ... villo' puts the shine in the wool itself — 'villus' is the shaggy nap of a hide. 'Minyae' is a standing name for the Argonauts, taken from the stock several of them were reckoned to come from. 'prima ... carina' is an ablative, 'in the first keel', with the keel standing for the whole ship: the Argo was held to be the first ship ever built, which is what makes 'non notum' literal rather than decorative — nobody had been over that sea because nobody had been over any sea. The part ends with the two winged brothers going out on it.
